One game, small boards, Elo anchored to a perfect player, and no uncertainty on the fitted trade-off coefficients. | Read |
| [NOTE-885](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-885.md) | Dwork, Kim, Reingold, Rothblum & Yona — Outcome Indistinguishability | A predictor p̃ is outcome indistinguishable (OI) relative to a class A of distinguishers when no A ∈ A can tell an individual with Nature's outcome from the same individual with an outcome drawn from Ber(p̃_i). The paper sets out four levels by how much access the distinguisher has to p̃: none, the prediction on the sampled individual, oracle queries, or the code. The lower two levels are equivalent to multi-accuracy and multi-calibration over closely related classes. At those levels OI predictors exist with size O(s/ε²), whatever Nature's complexity. At the oracle level, under fine-grained hardness of clique counting or BPP ≠ PSPACE, some efficient distinguisher classes force any OI predictor to be nearly as expensive as Nature's own predictor. That gives a strict separation between oracle access and sample access. OI never requires p̃ ≈ p*. A predictor is good only relative to A, and with the paper's construction a weak A gives a coarse predictor that a richer A would refute. The paper covers binary outcomes, a fixed representation of individuals and single samples (multi-sample OI is left mostly to future work). | Read |
| [NOTE-910](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-910.md) | Indyk & Xu — Worst-case performance of popular approximate nearest neighbor search implementations | For DiskANN's "slow preprocessing" graph (each point linked to the points that survive α-pruning of all other points, naively O(n³) time), greedy search from any start with no backtracking reaches a ((α+1)/(α−1) + ε)-approximate nearest neighbour in O(log_α(∆/((α−1)ε))) steps, each costing O((4α)^d log ∆) for doubling dimension d and aspect ratio ∆; the ratio is tight and the dependence on ∆ cannot be replaced by log n. For DiskANN with its practical "fast preprocessing", HNSW, NSG and seven other graph indexes, the paper constructs two-dimensional point sets (constant doubling dimension) on which, in experiments with the authors' code at the authors' recommended parameters, the search queue must hold about 10% of the points before recall@5 becomes non-zero or the approximation ratio becomes reasonable. The linear lower bounds are empirical, for one query per constructed instance, with an informal Ω(n/R) argument for fast-preprocessing DiskANN; no theorem bounds HNSW or NSG. | Read |
| [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md) | Malkov & Yashunin — Hierarchical navigable small world graphs for approximate nearest neighbour search | HNSW is a stack of proximity graphs on nested random subsets of the data. Each element's top layer is drawn from a geometric distribution, and new neighbours are chosen by a pruning rule that favours diverse directions. Searching from the sparse top layer down makes per-query cost grow about logarithmically with N on uniform random data in 4 and 8 dimensions, which flat NSW graphs did not. The logarithmic bound is derived only for exact Delaunay graphs of bounded mean degree, which HNSW does not build. For the graphs it does build, logarithmic scaling is measured, at low dimension only, and on 200M SIFT vectors the paper reports the scaling "deviates from the pure logarithm". The neighbour-selection rule is what keeps clustered data searchable: in the paper's synthetic test with 100 isolated clusters, linking each element to its nearest neighbours fails to reach high recall. There is no worst-case or recall guarantee, no deletion, and no analysis of query distributions unlike the data. | Read |
| [NOTE-971](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-971.md) | Wiskott and Sejnowski — Slow feature analysis | Finds instantaneous functions y = g(x(t)) whose outputs vary as slowly as possible, minimizing ⟨ẏ²⟩ under zero mean, unit variance and decorrelation. Over a fixed nonlinear expansion (all monomials of degree one and two), the problem is solved in closed form by sphering and then taking the smallest eigenvectors of the derivative covariance, a generalized eigenproblem. Stacked modules learn translation, size, rotation, contrast and, less well, illumination invariance for 1-D patterns, depending only on the training stimulus. The closed form is proved; everything about invariance, generalization and hierarchy is demonstrated on synthetic signals. The premise that slower means more abstract is assumed, not shown, and no generative model is used. | Read |
| [NOTE-981](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-981.md) | Charvin, Catenacci Volpi and Polani — Exact and soft successive refinement of the IB | Defines successive refinement for the information bottleneck as extending a coarse optimum T₁ to a fine optimum (T₁, S), and shows it equivalent to some pair of optima forming X → T₂ → T₁. With an injective fine decoder, it is also equivalent to the coarse decoder points lying in the convex hull of the fine ones, which a linear programme checks. Refinability is proved for binary X and Y, for Y a function of X, and for jointly Gaussian variables. Numerically the hull test on computed optima often fails, and the loss, measured by unique information, stays under a few percent. Those failures are uncertified. Run here with certified optima, the test shows that the four-state source of [CLAIM-387](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-387.md) is not refinable between β = 8 and β = 12: its stochastic optima do not nest either. | Read |
| [NOTE-983](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-983.md) | Rahaman et al. — On the Spectral Bias of Neural Networks | A ReLU network is piecewise linear, so its Fourier transform falls as k^(−d−1) along almost every direction and as k^(−2) along the normals to the faces of its linear regions; that is proved for compactly supported networks only. Trained networks fit low frequencies first, even when high frequencies carry ten times the amplitude, and high-frequency components are the first to be destroyed by parameter noise; both are experiments. The tie from the decay to the order of learning is a heuristic bound, and the volume "proof" in Appendix D does not hold. On a curve embedded in the plane, high latent frequencies are fitted more easily as the curve gets more petals. The paper puts this down to the shape of the curve, but most of it comes from the curve getting longer. | Read |
| [NOTE-984](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-984.md) | Coifman and Maggioni — Diffusion wavelets | A self-adjoint diffusion operator T with spectrum in [0, 1] defines a multiresolution analysis by thresholding its dyadic powers at a precision ε: V_j is spanned by the eigenvectors with λ^{t_j} ≥ ε, so the V_j are exactly nested spectral subspaces and the wavelet spaces W_j are spectral bands, about one octave of the generator each. The paper's contribution is an algorithm that builds localized orthonormal bases for approximations of these spaces without computing eigenvectors, by squaring the operator on each compressed basis. As written, that algorithm thresholds T^{2^{j−1}}, not T^{2^j−1} as the paper states, and the paper's own Fig. 9 follows the former. Localization, stability and the near-linear complexity are argued or observed, not proved for the compressed algorithm. | Read |
| [NOTE-985](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-985.md) | Coifman and Lafon — Diffusion maps | A symmetric non-negative kernel normalized into a reversible Markov chain gives a family of diffusion distances D_t, one per number of steps t, and an embedding by eigenvectors weighted by λ_l^t in which Euclidean distance is D_t. An α-normalization by a kernel density estimate makes the small-bandwidth limit the graph Laplacian with a density potential (α = 0), the Langevin generator whose invariant density is the sampling density (α = 1/2) or the Laplace–Beltrami operator (α = 1). The truncation is claimed accurate to relative precision δ, which is wrong: the bound is absolute. Several displays carry errors, and the heat-kernel proof has a gap. | Read |
| [NOTE-986](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-986.md) | Nadler, Lafon, Coifman and Kevrekidis — Diffusion maps and reaction coordinates | Ties diffusion maps to the dynamics that generated the data. For samples from p = e^{−U}, the small-ε generator of the α-normalized walk is Δψ − 2(1 − α)∇ψ·∇U: the graph Laplacian (α = 0) gives Fokker–Planck with potential 2U, α = 1/2 gives the Langevin dynamics with potential U itself, and α = 1 gives Laplace–Beltrami. So the slow eigenfunctions of the α = 1/2 map approximate the slow modes of the sampled stochastic system, and the paper proposes them as reaction coordinates. The expansions are formal, and with the paper's kernel every printed generator is too large by a factor of two. Its double-well example is separable. From equilibrium samples the slow eigenfunction is recovered well and the slow eigenvalue is not. That slow eigenfunctions are closed in mean, and in law only under a condition, is the record's addition. | Read |
| [NOTE-1015](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1015.md) | Schüler and Wiskott — Slow feature analysis as variational inference | Under a Gaussian random-walk prior on the latents and an encoder N(g(x_t), I) that sees one time step, the ELBO is a per-point reconstruction term minus half the unordered slowness loss, an exact identity (up to a constant the paper drops by a slip). The reconstruction term stands in for SFA's constraints, by argument. In the linear case the paper gives only a necessary condition; solving it here shows the optimum recovers SFA's slow span on whitened input, cut at lag-one autocorrelation ½, with no basis or order, and departs from SFA on raw input. Its two-sentence account of Turner and Sahani is not a substitute for reading them. | Read |
| [NOTE-1024](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1024.md) | U.S. Copyright Office — Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 3: Generative AI Training | Training copies works at every input step, so the copy trigger fires and everything turns on fair use. Weights count as copies only of works they can regenerate. Under Warhol the training use is judged by its ultimate purpose: often transformative for a general model, barely so for one that serves the originals' audience. Expression, not just ideas, is learned, and machine learning is not human learning. Market dilution by same-kind outputs is harm. Licensing should develop without intervention. | Read |
| [NOTE-1033](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1033.md) | Kleinberg and Raghavan — Algorithmic monoculture and social welfare | Two firms each hire the best available candidate by either a private noisy ranking or one shared algorithmic ranking. If, at equal accuracy, a second mover prefers an independent ranking (preference for the first position) and is better off after a less accurate competitor (preference for weaker competition), then for every human accuracy there is a more accurate algorithm that both firms strictly prefer to use, yet both are worse off, and so is welfare, than if neither used it. The Mallows model meets the conditions for every candidate distribution; Gaussian and Laplacian random utility models meet them for three candidates; Plackett–Luce never does. | Read |
| [NOTE-1044](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1044.md) | Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner and Hardt — Performative prediction | When a deployed model's predictions change the distribution they are scored on, D(θ), two solution concepts separate: a performative optimum minimizes the risk on the distribution it induces, and a performatively stable point is optimal for the distribution it induces, a fixed point of retraining. With a β-jointly smooth, γ-strongly convex loss and a map D(·) that is ε-Lipschitz in Wasserstein-1, retraining contracts at rate εβ/γ and converges to a unique stable point when ε < γ/β, and removing any one condition can break convergence. Stable points and optima are within 2L_zε/γ of each other, and can differ. | Read |
| [NOTE-1048](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1048.md) | Xu, Zhao, Song, Stewart and Ermon — A theory of usable information under computational constraints | Defines predictive V-information, I_V(X → Y) = H_V(Y \| ∅) − H_V(Y \| X), where each V-entropy is the least expected log loss a predictor in the family V can reach. With V unrestricted it is Shannon mutual information; with linear-Gaussian V it is R² times the variance. It is non-negative and zero under independence because V must be able to ignore its input. Unlike Shannon information it can be asymmetric and can be raised by computing on X, and its empirical estimate is within 4R(G_V) + 2B√(2 log(1/δ)/N) of the truth with probability 1 − 2δ. It is not bounded by Shannon information unless V's input-free predictions can match the marginal of Y. | Read |
| [NOTE-1049](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1049.md) | Kay, Kasirzadeh and Mohamed — Epistemic injustice in generative AI | A conceptual taxonomy, illustrated with reported cases, of four ways generative models can take part in epistemic injustice: amplified and manipulative testimonial injustice, hermeneutical ignorance and access injustice. Its sharpest move is to relocate the testimonial wrong: in the algorithmic setting it "requires a credibility excess assigned to the algorithm". It counts deliberate fabrication as testimonial injustice, which Fricker's account sets apart, and stretches hermeneutical injustice to unequal access to information. Nothing in it is measured by the authors. | Read |
| [NOTE-1069](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1069.md) | Gurnee — Verbalizable representations form a global workspace in language models | A corpus-averaged Jacobian lens picks out, in each layer of Claude models, the directions a model is disposed to verbalize. Swaps, injections and ablations along these directions (the J-space) show them privileged for report, held concepts, two-hop reasoning and reuse of an argument by many functions, while continuation, anomaly detection and line wrapping use the same information without them. The J-space works in a middle band of layers, carries under 10% of activation variance, and is amplified and relayed by the weights more than other directions. Ablating it flattens experiential language about the self and about others. The authors take no position on phenomenal consciousness. | Read |
| [NOTE-1091](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1091.md) | Aevyra — The Ledger of Will | A careful, self-limiting formal note on what a reduced memory must keep so that an agent can still revise: a retained state supports a declared family of future questions, interventions and changes of evaluative law exactly when those targets are constant on its fibres, and under repeated revision exactly when its fibres lie in the coarsest revision-invariant refinement (Moore–Nerode). The rest is design proposal and an unexecuted experimental protocol. Elementary and correct; the authors say plainly that it synthesizes established ideas. | Read |
| [NOTE-1099](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1099.md) | Statistical ranking and combinatorial Hodge theory | Rank aggregation as combinatorial Hodge theory. Aggregated pairwise comparisons form an edge flow, and its orthogonal decomposition gives a least-squares global ranking (the gradient), local inconsistency (curl) and global inconsistency (harmonic). The size of the cyclic residual certifies whether any global ranking is meaningful. The framework is cardinal, generalizes Borda, and is not Kemeny. | Read |
| [NOTE-1116](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1116.md) | Flows and Decompositions of Games: Harmonic and Potential Games | A finite game is read as a flow, the unilateral payoff differences on the graph of strategy profiles, and the Helmholtz decomposition of that flow splits the game uniquely into potential, harmonic and nonstrategic parts. Potential games are those with no harmonic part. Harmonic games, the pure-conflict part, generically have no pure equilibrium. The nearest potential game is a closed-form l2 projection. | Read |
| [NOTE-1130](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1130.md) | Gerstner et al. — Eligibility traces and plasticity on behavioral time scales | A review by theoreticians. In a three-factor rule, pre- and postsynaptic co-activation sets a decaying synaptic flag, the eligibility trace, and the weight changes only if a third signal (reward minus expected reward, surprise, novelty, or a neuron-specific error) arrives while it is set. Five experimental papers (2014–2017), mostly in slices, give traces of about 1 s in striatum, 3–10 s in cortex, about 2 s and about a minute in hippocampus. The authors grant that other mechanisms could bridge the same gap. | Read |
| [NOTE-1132](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1132.md) | Soma et al. — The hive mind is a single reinforcement learning agent | A short theoretical paper with simulations. In an infinite, well-mixed population, imitation of success has the expected update of Cross Learning, and the weighted voter model of the honey-bee waggle dance that of Maynard-Cross Learning, the Maynard-Smith replicator dynamic. The population's type distribution is the policy of a stateless bandit agent, each member is one parallel sample of it, and no member learns. The authors keep the biology partial and the simulations qualitative. | Read |
| [NOTE-1140](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1140.md) | Kaisers & Tuyls — Frequency adjusted multi-agent Q-learning | A short algorithmic paper with plotted experiments. The selection–mutation model of Boltzmann Q-learning (Tuyls et al. 2003, 2005) assumes every Q-value changes at rate α; in Q-learning only the chosen action's does, so its expected change carries a factor x_i, and Q-learning departs from the model depending on initialization. A frequency-adjusted update removes the factor and matches the model. Three 2×2 games, one temperature, no quantitative measure of fit. | Read |
| [NOTE-1141](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1141.md) | Son et al. — QTRAN: learning to factorize with transformation | Defines Individual-Global-Max (IGM): per-agent values factorise a joint value when the profile of individual argmaxes is the joint argmax. Additivity and monotonicity are sufficient conditions; QTRAN trains the sum of individual values plus a state value to equal the joint value at the greedy profile and bound it elsewhere, which is sufficient and, up to rescaling, necessary. Every single-state matrix game satisfies IGM; VDN and QMIX missed the optimum in 177 of 310 random 3×3 games. | Read |
| [NOTE-1142](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1142.md) | Hart & Mas-Colell — A simple adaptive procedure leading to correlated equilibrium | A theorem with a proof. Regret matching, switching from one's last action to each alternative with probability proportional to the positive regret for not having made that switch in the past, drives the empirical joint distribution of play almost surely to the set of correlated equilibria when every player uses it. Regrets vanish exactly when the empirical distribution approaches that set. A stylized variant is analysed by Blackwell approachability; the main procedure needs inertia and needs players to see one another's past play. | Read |
| [NOTE-1143](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1143.md) | Balduzzi et al. — Open-ended learning in symmetric zero-sum games | A framework paper with an algorithm and two small experiments. Symmetric zero-sum games between parametrized agents split into transitive and cyclic parts relative to a measure on agents. In a cyclic game an individual's performance is meaningless, so evaluation moves to populations: the value of the game between them, which is invariant to redundant members, and the convex hull of their evaluation rows. Training each supported agent on what it beats grows that hull. | Read |
| [NOTE-1144](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1144.md) | Sato & Crutchfield — Coupled replicator equations for the dynamics of learning in multiagent systems | A four-page letter. Two agents choose by softmax over reward memories that decay at rate α; with learning slow relative to play, each agent's choice distribution follows a replicator dynamic in the other's play plus α Σ_j x_j log(x_j/x_i), a pull towards uniform play. Without decay the system is conservative, Hamiltonian in zero-sum games; with decay it is dissipative. Rock–scissors–paper simulations show tori, Hamiltonian chaos, heteroclinic transients, limit cycles and chaotic attractors. Derivation plus numerics, no data. | Read |
| [NOTE-1145](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1145.md) | Shazeer et al. — Outrageously large neural networks: the sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts layer | An engineering paper with large experiments. A sparsely-gated layer of up to 131,072 experts raises capacity over 1000-fold at roughly constant computation. Read here for one observation and one fix: without constraint the gate concentrates on a few experts, which the authors call self-reinforcing, and two auxiliary losses that penalize unequal importance and load remove it, which in one ablation also improves perplexity from 39.8 to 35.6. | Read |
| [NOTE-1146](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1146.md) | Czarnecki et al. — Real world games look like spinning tops | A hypothesis paper with theorems and sampled empirical games. Where players can signal n bits before the outcome is settled, every win–loss pattern on 2ⁿ strategies occurs, so cycles are astronomically long. Nash clustering layers any symmetric zero-sum game, and beating a whole cluster guarantees climbing. Sampled games show cluster size peaking at middling strength. The body says the geometry is not proved, the abstract says it is. Two of the smaller results have defective statements or proofs. | Read |
| [NOTE-1147](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1147.md) | Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan and Hinton — Adaptive mixtures of local experts | A short paper that founds the mixture of experts. Scoring the error of a single, gate-selected expert, or the mixture's negative log-likelihood, makes experts compete for cases, and an expert better than the gate-weighted average gains responsibility for the case. On a vowel task 4 or 8 linear experts learned in half the epochs of matched backpropagation networks at equal accuracy, divided the task by class pair, and left all but 2 or 3 experts with mixing proportion near zero. | Read |
| [NOTE-1148](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1148.md) | Yang et al. — Mean field multi-agent reinforcement learning | An algorithms paper with a convergence proof and three experiments. Each agent's Q-function is approximated by its interaction with the mean action of its neighbours, which makes many-agent RL tractable for hundreds of homogeneous agents. Mean field Q-learning converges to a Nash Q-value under strong assumptions, learns Gaussian Squeeze with 500 and 1000 agents where baselines fail, matches MCMC on a 20 × 20 Ising model, and wins a 64-versus-64 battle game. | Read |
| [NOTE-1150](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1150.md) | Foerster et al. — Learning with opponent-learning awareness | A LOLA learner maximises its return after the opponent's anticipated naive gradient step and differentiates through that step, adding a second-order term to its gradient. Two exact-gradient LOLA learners reached tit-for-tat-like reciprocity in the memory-one iterated prisoner's dilemma where naive learners ended at mutual defection, and settled at the mixed equilibrium of iterated matching pennies where naive learners did not converge. A policy-gradient version cooperated in the Coin Game, less reliably with a learned model of the opponent. | Read |
| [NOTE-1151](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1151.md) | Leibo et al. — Multi-agent reinforcement learning in sequential social dilemmas | A descriptive simulation study. It defines sequential social dilemmas, Markov games whose learned cooperative and defecting policies give social-dilemma payoffs, and runs independent deep Q-learners on two two-player games. Scarcity and costly conflict produce aggression in Gathering; group benefit produces joint hunting in Wolfpack; and network size moves defection in opposite directions in two games that both embed a Prisoner's Dilemma. | Read |
| [NOTE-1152](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1152.md) | Foerster et al. — Counterfactual multi-agent policy gradients | A centralised critic Q(s, τ, u) trains decentralised actors, and each agent's action is scored against the critic's average over its own alternatives under its own policy, the others' actions fixed. The baseline does not change the expected gradient. On StarCraft micromanagement with a narrow field of view it beat independent and central-V/QV actor-critics on four maps. The counterfactual is the critic's estimate, not a simulation, and it values alternatives the agents sometimes take. | Read |
| [NOTE-1153](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1153.md) | Wolpert & Tumer — Optimal reward functions in distributed reinforcement learning | Members of a collective each run a reinforcement learner on a private utility, and the designer wants the world utility G maximised. A private utility is factored when it orders a member's own alternatives, others fixed, as G does; this holds exactly when it is an increasing function of G given what the member cannot affect. The Wonderful Life Utility, G minus G with the member's effect set clamped, is factored and easier to learn than G. In a 60-agent bar problem, clamping to the average action did best, clamping to absence nearly as well, G worst. | Read |
| [NOTE-1154](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1154.md) | Rashid et al. — QMIX: monotonic value function factorisation | Per-agent values Q_a(τ^a, u^a) are combined into a joint Q_tot by a mixing network whose weights, generated from the state, are kept non-negative, so ∂Q_tot/∂Q_a ≥ 0. Then the individually greedy actions form a greedy joint action and agents can act on their own values. It represents more than a sum and learned the optimum of a two-step game that a sum misses; it cannot represent a joint value in which one agent's best action depends on the others' current actions. | Read |
| [NOTE-1155](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1155.md) | Balduzzi et al. — Re-evaluating evaluation | A methods paper with two short applications. It reads evaluation data as antisymmetric matrices. Elo is then the row mean of the log-odds, exact when they are curl-free and movable by copies, and the Schur decomposition gives a multidimensional Elo. Nash averaging scores agents and tasks against the maximum-entropy Nash equilibrium of a zero-sum meta-game. Its proved invariance covers exact copies, and only when that equilibrium is unique. A checked counterexample shows what happens otherwise. | Read |
| [NOTE-1156](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1156.md) | Omidshafiei et al. — α-Rank: multi-agent evaluation by evolution | A methods paper with theory and applications. Agents are ranked by the stationary distribution of a finite-population, rare-mutation Fermi imitation chain on pure profiles, unique at every finite α. As α grows its transitions become those of Markov-Conley chains, the sinks of the better-response graph, which the paper ties to chain components of the replicator flow. The limit of the ranking is not characterized, and it is not invariant to copies. | Read |
